blocks.text: “The forefeet are set immediately behind the neck; they are very short, roundish and almost naked, and never touch the ground. It keeps them always tucked under the neck, in place of hands, so that they are scarcely visible. — It moves on its hind feet alone, and so walks by leaping.” These are the words of Hasselquist, p. 278.

“The tail is faintly quadrangular, of even thickness and very long (three times longer than the body). It is covered with very short, stiff hairs, and over the last three inches it is set with long, rather soft, distinct hairs.” Hasselquist p. 279.

“The colour of the head, and of the body down to the middle of the flanks, is pale brown. The rest of the flanks and the belly are white. White hairs arranged in a small arc bound the body immediately above the tail. The tail is pale brown. The end of the tail, which is the most hairy part, is black above the tip, but the very tip is white. The ears and feet are flesh-coloured.” Hasselquist ibid.
This cleverness of the animal is also attested by more recent writers; see Oedmann IV, p. 53. 54.

This, however, is flatly denied by Shaw, Travels p. 157, German trans., and by Bruce, Travels vol. 5, p. 132. Oedmann, IV, p. 51. 52, seeks the cause of this disagreement between the ancients and the moderns in the fact that the Arabs were accustomed to use their يربوع [yarbūʿ] for two species of two-footed mouse: both for the one that Linnaeus calls mus iaculus and Pallas mus sagitta, which digs its nests in shifting sand and sandy plains, and for another, smaller one, unknown to Linnaeus, called mus iaculus by Pallas and Siberian Ierbua by Pennant, which makes its dwellings in firm ground. Oedmann holds that the Hebrews too comprised both these species under the single name שפן, and a certain learned man agrees with him in the Notes on Bruce's Travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 159. But when Oedmann thinks that the second species of two-footed mouse, Pennant's Iarbua Sibirica, is the same as the animal that Shaw describes under the name lamb of the Israelites, he was without doubt mistaken. For it is clear from what Bochart cited from the Arabs above, p. 1005, that غنم بني اسرايل [ghanam banī isrāyil] is synonymous with وبر [wabr], which, as we saw above in note 3, is the name of the hyrax, or Syrian shrew.

Since each of these features is found no less in the hyrax, or Syrian shrew (see above, note 3), Arab. وبر [wabr], it is highly doubtful which animal the Hebrew שפן signifies. [II, 428] The ancients, however, seem to side with the jerboa (mus iaculus), يربوع [yarbūʿ]; read what Bochart will shortly point out about their interpretations,

Another etymology is offered by the Arabic dialect, in which أَلشَّعْنُ [al-shaʿn] is أَلْكَيِّسُ أَلْعَاقِلُ [al-kayyis al-ʿāqil], astute, clever, as Giauhari explains it; his words are quoted by Schultens in Commentar. ad Prov. p. 483. This etymology favours the jerboa (mus iaculus), whose cleverness in preparing its dwelling we saw above, p. 1012.
